doc.title: Ellen Rowe interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 2, 2024

title: Band director father, high school, and landing the U Conn job
summary: Rowe grew up with instruments at home, had perfect pitch, was pushed into jazz at 14, went to Eastman, moved to New York, and got the U Conn job via Ray Wright while on a cruise ship.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Did you have that decision to make early on about oh I’m going to try to make a living just as a performer or no I like to teach so I’ll do both?

So my dad was a high school band director and there was lots of instruments laying around our house. I inherited perfect pitch from him and you know I thought I was being bad when parents were over the house and I was putting together all the instruments trying to figure out how to play them. You know I thought I was some kind of criminal. But so music came naturally to me as a child, which was great, I mean what a blessing. And then I kind of got into high school and I was just playing all the time, flute and piano, and taught myself bassoon because there was no bassoon players in the high school. But I think I kind of — my band director took me aside, because I was also an athlete and playing lots of sports. And he said, “You know you’re really going to have to make a choice right now, I mean if you’re going to continue on in music you need to start thinking seriously about auditions and going to music school and if sports are going to continue to occupy as much of your time as they are that’s going to be difficult.” So I didn’t give up sports but I kind of got my priorities realigned. And so I think at the time I assumed that I would just continue being a musician and see where it brought me, and music education was my best avenue to get into a school because I wasn’t a — you know my parents had never forced lessons on me except for the jazz lessons that I forced on myself at age — or my band director forced on me — at age 14 when he said, “If you’re going to play in my high school jazz band you are going to actually learn something about jazz.” And so off I went and then I just — wow, this is so exciting and cool. So this is a very long answer to your question, I apologize, but what I’m getting at is by the time I got to Eastman and started discovering jazz and realized that writing was something I apparently was reasonably good at and got to continue studying with Ray Wright I did finish up my music education degree and I did go out and do my student teaching. But then I moved to New York because I wanted to see what that was about. And I actually fell into my first college teaching job. It was really by accident. I was at the time thinking I was probably going to continue to just try to freelance and see where that took me. But I was working on the S.S. Norway on a cruise ship and I got a — I don’t know if it was a telegram at that time or what it was on board the ship — from Ray Wright saying that the University of Connecticut, where I grew up, was going to try to start a jazz program and they had an opening for a half time person and was I interested.
